title: Network Time Protocol Version 4: Protocol and Algorithms Specification
subtitle: How computers across the Internet agree on what time it is, to within milliseconds or better.
summary: NTP version 4 is the protocol that keeps computer clocks in step across the Internet. A client exchanges timestamped UDP packets with one or more servers, measures how far its clock is off and how long the round trip took, and then runs filtering, selection and clock-discipline algorithms to steer its clock smoothly toward the right time. This RFC specifies the packet format, the on-wire exchange and the algorithms, and obsoletes NTPv3 (RFC 1305) and SNTPv4 (RFC 4330).

eli5.summary: Your computer's clock slowly drifts, so it keeps asking a few clocks it trusts what time it is, works out how long the answers took to arrive, ignores any clock that disagrees with the rest, and nudges itself gently to match.

tldr.problem: Clocks on separate computers drift apart, and network delay makes it hard to tell how far off a clock really is.
tldr.mechanism: A client and server swap four timestamps in UDP packets, from which the client computes clock offset and round-trip delay. Filter, select, cluster and combine algorithms then pick the best sources and discipline the local clock.
tldr.outcome: Clients can hold accurate time over the public Internet, and NTPv4 is the specification most deployed NTP software follows.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) synchronizes the system clocks of a set of distributed time servers and clients. Version 4 describes the core architecture, protocol, state machines, data structures and algorithms. It builds on NTPv3 in RFC 1305 and takes in the simplified subset known as SNTPv4 from RFC 4330; this RFC obsoletes both. Changes to header fields are small enough that NTPv4 still interoperates with earlier versions.

NTP is a hierarchy. A few primary servers are synchronized by wire or radio to national time standards, and secondary servers and clients pull time from them, so values flow outward from the root. The algorithms are meant to cope with network disruption, server failure and hostile actions. The RFC says typical primary servers using modern machines are precise within a few tens of microseconds, and typical clients on fast LANs within a few hundred microseconds.

Appendix A of the RFC is a full skeleton program in C. It is explicitly non-normative: it illustrates the algorithms but is not a requirement for a conforming implementation.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school where every classroom clock must show the same time. One teacher has the official watch. Other teachers check with that teacher, and the students check with their teacher. The time spreads out from the official watch, and each room does its best to stay accurate even if the hallway is noisy.

sections.title: Modes and Strata
sections.content:
An NTP implementation acts as a primary server, a secondary server or a client. A primary server is synchronized to a reference clock traceable to UTC, such as GPS. A client synchronizes to one or more upstream servers but serves no one. A secondary server has both upstream and downstream peers.

The RFC defines three protocol variants. In client/server mode, the client pulls time from a server. In symmetric mode, two peers both push and pull. In broadcast mode, a server periodically sends packets that many clients can receive, and a broadcast server pushes synchronization to clients. There is also dynamic server discovery with manycast, where a client sends to a group address and suitable servers answer with ordinary server packets.

Every server has a stratum. Primary servers are stratum 1, and each step down the hierarchy adds one. In the packet, stratum 0 means unspecified or invalid, 1 a primary server, 2 to 15 a secondary server, and 16 unsynchronized; 17 to 255 are reserved. The RFC notes that the subnet topology is determined with a variant of the Bellman-Ford routing algorithm, which computes a shortest-path spanning tree rooted on the primary servers.
sections.eli5: Some clocks are the boss clocks, because they listen to a very exact source. Their helpers are one step away, their helpers' helpers are two steps away, and so on. The bigger the number, the farther you are from the boss clock, so the less you should trust it.

sections.title: Time Formats and Parameters
sections.content:
NTP uses three formats for time. The 64-bit timestamp is a 32-bit unsigned seconds field plus a 32-bit fraction, spanning 136 years at about 232 picosecond resolution. The 32-bit short format has 16 bits of seconds and 16 of fraction and is used for delay and dispersion fields. The 128-bit date format adds a 32-bit era number and a 32-bit era offset to a 64-bit fraction, for use where storage allows.

The prime epoch, the start of era 0, is 0 h on 1 January 1900 UTC, when all bits are zero. Era 0 runs until some time in 2036, when the timestamp wraps and era 1 begins. The RFC also notes that the Era Number cannot be produced by NTP directly; it must come from external means such as the filesystem or dedicated hardware. A timestamp of zero is a special case meaning unknown or unsynchronized time.

PORT 123
The well-known port assigned for NTP.
MINPOLL 4, MAXPOLL 17
Poll exponents: 2^4 = 16 seconds up to 2^17 seconds, about 36 hours.
MAXDIST 1, MAXSTRAT 16
A one-second distance threshold and the largest stratum number.
sections.eli5: NTP counts time in seconds since the start of 1900, plus a very tiny fraction of a second. The counter is so big it lasts about 136 years before it starts over, which will happen in 2036, so computers need a little extra help to know which lap they are on.

sections.title: The Packet Header
sections.content:
An NTP packet is a UDP datagram. The header is 12 32-bit words in network byte order, followed by optional extension fields and an optional message authentication code (MAC). The header holds a leap indicator (0 no warning, 1 last minute of the day has 61 seconds, 2 has 59 seconds, 3 unknown or unsynchronized clock), a 3-bit version number (4), a 3-bit mode, an 8-bit stratum, an 8-bit signed poll exponent and an 8-bit signed precision exponent, both in log2 seconds.

Root delay and root dispersion are 32-bit short-format values, giving the total round-trip delay and total dispersion to the reference clock. The 32-bit reference ID identifies the source. At stratum 1 it is a left-justified, zero-padded ASCII name such as GPS or PPS; above stratum 1 it is the upstream server's IPv4 address, or the first four octets of the MD5 hash of its IPv6 address, which helps detect timing loops. Four 64-bit timestamps follow: reference, origin, receive and transmit.

Modes are 1 symmetric active, 2 symmetric passive, 3 client, 4 server, 5 broadcast, 6 NTP control message and 7 reserved for private use; 0 is reserved. Extension fields have a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length and are zero-padded to a word boundary.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a postcard with a fixed set of boxes. There are boxes for how sure the sender is about its clock, how far it is from the boss clock, and four boxes where it writes times, so the receiver can see when things were sent and received.

sections.title: The On-Wire Exchange
sections.content:
The core of NTP is a timestamp exchange. A client sends a request and records the time t1 when it left. The server notes the time t2 when it arrived and t3 when its reply departed, and puts t1, t2 and t3 in the reply. The client records t4 on arrival. From the four timestamps (T1 to T4) the client computes the offset of the server relative to itself and the round-trip delay:

offset = 1/2 * [(T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)]
delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2)

The delay subtracts the time the server spent holding the packet, so only the network travel remains. The offset assumes the outbound and return paths take about equally long. Because the protocol depends only on measured offsets, it does not need reliable delivery; the RFC even observes that TCP retries would make NTP packets less reliable, since they would add to the measured delay.

Two sanity checks protect against duplicate, bogus or replayed packets, using the origin and transmit timestamps. The RFC also warns that the client must be set within 34 years of the server before the service starts, a limit of 64-bit integer arithmetic; floating-point arithmetic restores 68 years. If a computed delay would be negative, it is clamped to at least the system precision.
sections.eli5: You send a letter that says what time you mailed it. Your friend writes down when it arrived and when they mailed their answer. When you get the reply you know four times, so you can work out how long the mail took and how far apart your two clocks are.

sections.title: Filtering, Selection and Discipline
sections.content:
Raw samples are noisy, so NTPv4 grooms them in stages. The clock filter keeps the most recent samples from each server in an 8-stage shift register and prefers those with the lowest delay. It also derives dispersion, jitter and a synchronization distance, lambda = delta/2 + epsilon. A server whose distance exceeds MAXDIST (1 s) is considered unfit for synchronization.

The system process then combines all sources. The selection algorithm, modified from Marzullo's work, looks for an intersection interval holding a majority clique of truechimers and rejects falsetickers. The cluster algorithm discards statistical outliers, and the system keeps at least NMIN (3) survivors in its parameters. The combine algorithm produces the best and final offset.

Finally the clock discipline feeds that offset into a feedback loop that mixes a phase-locked loop and a frequency-locked loop. The RFC says a PLL usually works better when network jitter dominates and an FLL when oscillator wander dominates. The clock-adjust process then slews the system clock. A separate poll process sets how often each server is queried.
sections.eli5: If you ask five clocks for the time and one says something silly, you throw that answer away. You keep the ones that agree, average the best, and then speed up or slow down your own clock a tiny bit instead of jumping, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Kiss-o'-Death, SNTP and IANA
sections.content:
When a packet has stratum 0, the reference ID carries a four-character ASCII kiss code instead of a clock name. These Kiss-o'-Death (KoD) packets let a server tell a client to behave. Receivers must inspect them: for DENY and RSTR the client must demobilize its associations to that server and stop sending to it; for RATE it must immediately reduce its polling interval and keep reducing it on each further RATE code. Codes beginning with "X" are for experimentation and are ignored if not recognized. The Receive and Transmit Timestamps in a KoD packet are undefined and must be discarded.

Other defined codes include ACST, AUTH, AUTO, BCST, CRYP, DROP, INIT, MCST, NKEY, RMOT and STEP.

Simple NTP (SNTPv4) is a subset of the same protocol, intended for primary servers with a single reference clock and for clients with a single upstream server and no dependents. These do not need the mitigation algorithms. Other than that, NTP and SNTP are fully interoperable and can be mixed in one network.

IANA assigned UDP/TCP port 123, the IPv4 multicast group 224.0.1.1 and an IPv6 multicast address ending :101 to NTP. It also created registries for Extension Field Types, Reference Identifier codes and Kiss-o'-Death codes, and is asked never to assign a code beginning with "X". RFC 9748 later updated those registries.
sections.eli5:
Sometimes a server says, "Please stop asking so often," using a short code word instead of the time. A polite client listens: it asks less often, or stops asking that server entirely.

The official lists of NTP's port number and code words are kept by IANA.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls NTP's security requirements "even more stringent than most other distributed services", because authentication and time are intertwined: keys are valid only for set intervals, yet enforcing intervals needs a trustworthy clock. Built-in defenses include the on-wire timestamp scheme, which resists spoofing, packet loss and replay, and the filter, selection and clustering algorithms, which defend against Byzantine falsetickers. But these mechanisms do not securely identify and authenticate servers to clients.

This document specifies the symmetric-key MAC, carried over from NTPv3: a 32-bit key identifier plus a 128-bit MD5 digest. Public-key authentication, Autokey, is specified separately in RFC 5906. The RFC acknowledges the known weaknesses of MD5 but says its use is consistent with wide deployment.

The RFC says the on-wire protocol does not resist replay of a client request packet, which yields a server reply with new T2 and T3 and an incorrect offset and delay. Setting the xmt state variable to zero after computing offset and delay avoids this.

Broadcast clients are vulnerable to hostile broadcast servers; filtering and cryptographic authentication reduce that risk. Later documents update NTPv4 here, notably RFC 8573 for the MAC and RFC 9109 for port randomization.
sections.eli5: If a stranger shouts the wrong time, your clock could be fooled. NTP has several ways to catch bad answers, and a secret password can prove who is talking, but the original password method is old, so newer documents improved it.

today: NTPv4 is still the base specification for NTP, and the protocol is how most servers, desktops and network devices keep their clocks accurate. Several later RFCs update this one rather than replace it, covering extension fields, MAC algorithms, port randomization, registries and interleaved modes. The well-known reference implementation is available at ntp.org, which the RFC itself cites, and other widely used implementations such as chrony also speak NTP.
